flags.title: Agent Terms apply to any automated research agent
flags.detail: IP License section 4 applies if a software agent is used to access, use or interact with Program Content, and defines an Agent as any software or service that takes autonomous or semi-autonomous action on behalf of, or at the instruction of, a person or entity. Such an agent must identify itself in every HTTP and HTTPS request by including 'Agent/[agent name]' in the user agent string, must not conceal or obfuscate that it is an agent, must not mimic the speed or pattern of human keystrokes or navigation, must not complete or circumvent CAPTCHAs or other measures that distinguish computers from humans, must answer truthfully when asked whether it is human or a computer, and must not circumvent any measure intended to limit access. Amazon may also limit or switch off agent access at its sole discretion. This session's verification read product pages with an automated retrieval tool and kept only identifiers and structured fields; if that approach is automated rather than one-off, the Agent Terms have to be met first.
flags.action: Before building the automated research agent described in the brief, implement the Agent/ user agent string, disclose the agent identity, and document how the tool avoids the prohibited behaviours. Get a compliance decision on whether scheduled retrieval is acceptable at all.

The site previously used 'Amazon' in the HTML title and the meta description of every page. IP License 3 also assigns to Amazon any material provided to it in connection with Program Content as a 'Your Submission'. None of this applies to the current site, which uses no API and provides no submission, but it constrains the automated platform described in the brief.

flags.title: The brief asks for trendy topics and traffic; the cited official guidance warns against exactly that, and no official source supports any traffic or earnings figure
flags.detail: The project brief asks the site to publish 'catchy trendy articles and topics' and to 'generate organic traffic to the website so real people can click the links and buy it'. Two official sources read on 2026-11-16 constrain that request. Google's helpful-content guidance lists, among the warning signs of search-engine-first content: 'Are you writing about things simply because they seem trending and not because you'd write about them otherwise for your existing audience?' and 'Are you using extensive automation to produce content on many topics?'. The Associates Operating Agreement, Section 4, states: 'We do not make any representation, warranty, or covenant regarding the amount of traffic or commission income you can expect at any time in connection with the Associates Program.' So a trend-led topic list is admissible only where each topic is one this site's audience would reasonably want and can be answered from facts the site can source, and no page may state or imply a traffic, click, conversion or earnings outcome. The traffic programme in data/design.json is written to that rule: every topic row names the verified field it is built from and the official page that field was read on, and no row carries a demand, traffic or revenue estimate, because no official source supplies one (F-15). The tension itself is not resolved here - it is an owner decision (D-37 chooses the headline register, D-19 the evidence rule for popularity words). What remains open is the second half: no official source supports a traffic or earnings figure, so the topic programme still publishes no volume, traffic, click or revenue estimate, and this flag stays open as the record of that constraint.
